title: edge-router-topology-and-egress-zones
content:
Purpose / summary:
This note captures proposed topology and operational tradeoffs for how Redwood will place and route traffic at the edge across multiple regions, how egress zones should be defined/owned, and where mTLS termination and service-mesh responsibilities live. Goal is to provide a single-page-ish decision log for platform engineers and SREs preparing the Q1 rollout of multi-region private deployments.

Context / constraints:
- Customers expect predictable latency and deterministic failover when a region goes into maintenance or has capacity issues.
- Some customers will use Redwood Private in air-gapped or VPC-contained environments; others will use Dedicated with reserved capacity.
- Regulatory requirements force some egress (to telemetry, updates, or 3rd-party partners) to be constrained to specific regions or peered networks.
- Cost: cross-region egress and inter-region traffic is material; we must minimize unnecessary hairpinning through central control planes.
- Security: zero-trust posture, mutual auth for control-plane-to-data-plane communications, and auditability of egress decisions.

High-level topology options considered (and recommendation):
1) Regional gateways + Anycasted edge entry (recommended hybrid)
   - Deploy regional gateway fleets per cloud region; advertise a global Anycast IP per customer or global frontend to push traffic to the nearest healthy gateway.
   - Each regional gateway performs protocol termination (TLS), basic authentication, rate limiting, and routes final traffic to local cluster mesh or to other regions based on policy.
   - Advantages: low-latency ingress, region-local policy enforcement, simpler egress accounting.
   - Disadvantages: global config distribution complexity, potential cross-region request routing for stateful sessions.

2) Centralized front-door + regional backends
   - Single control entry (or small active/passive pair) terminates traffic and proxies to regional backends.
   - Too many cross-region hops -> higher cost and worse p99 latency.

3) Pure regional with DNS steering (no Anycast)
   - Use low-TTL DNS and geo-DNS to steer clients. Simple but slower failover and less deterministic for mobile clients.

Routing policy primitives we will support:
- Region-preferred with spillover: prefer local region; spill to secondary regions only when capacity or explicit health checks fail.
- Cost-aware routing: prefer cheaper region when latency delta within X ms.
- Customer-binding: route specific customers to pinned regions for compliance.
- Canary: route N% of traffic to new region/model variant for rollouts.

Egress zones and policy model:
- Define an "egress zone" as: region + logical egress group (e.g., telemetry, third-party-apis, data-warehouse) + allowed exit network ranges.
- Zones are owned by Platform Networking (config) and enforced at gateway or egress-gateway sidecars.
- Rules include: allowed destinations, forced SNAT ranges, DLP/proxy inspection flags, and required ACL exceptions.
- Default behavior: local egress for most traffic. Non-local egress only with explicit policy or automated reroute under failover.

mTLS / termination decision matrix:
- Option A: Terminate mTLS at the edge gateway (recommended for customer-facing TLS)
  - Pros: simpler certificate lifecycle, edge can validate client certs and apply per-customer policies.
  - Cons: requires secure channel from gateway -> mesh/sidecar to preserve end-to-end auth semantics.

- Option B: Passthrough TLS to sidecars/service mesh (recommended for intra-tenant private deployments)
  - Pros: preserves end-to-end identity, minimizes gateway responsibilities.
  - Cons: complex for public hosted API where we need to validate tokens early.

- Hybrid: edge terminates TLS, re-mTLSs to downstream service mesh with per-hop certs issued by our control-plane CA. This gives us observability at edge and zero-trust internally.

Service mesh interplay and sidecar responsibilities:
- Mesh responsibility: service-to-service auth, circuit-breaking, retry semantics, telemetry tags, fine-grained routing by header/metadata.
- Gateways should be lightweight: L7 routing, authn/authz pre-checks, rate limit, shaping. Avoid embedding complex mesh logic into gateway to keep restart/fail domains small.
- Sidecar/mesh should support "egress-gateway mode" where certain destinations leave the mesh via a dedicated egress cluster that enforces NAT and DLP.

Control plane topology (central vs distributed):
- Control-plane tasks: cert issuance (CA), config distribution, policy evaluation, telemetry ingestion and query.
- Recommendation: distributed control-plane with a regional control-plane instance that owns regional runtime config and policy evaluation; a lightweight global control-plane handles global policy, account metadata, and discovery.
  - Regional c-plane reduces latency for fetching config and certs, and reduces blast radius of outages.
  - Global plane provides consistency and cross-region rollouts.

Traffic steering and failover mechanics:
- Passive health checks + active probing from edge -> backend cluster to inform routing decisions.
- Fast failover path: if local gateway can't reach regional mesh for N consecutive checks, circuit to secondary region with active congestion control.
- State handling: prefer sticky session key hashing over IP-based affinity; for long-running streams (LLM sessions) route by session id hashed to region to avoid mid-stream reroute.

Operational controls and SLOs:
- p50/p95/p99 targets per region (ingress gateway latency) and cross-region failover SLO (time to switch < 15s on health failure).
- Egress cost SLO: maintain cross-region egress below Y% of total traffic for <95% of customers; alerts when exceeded.
- Security SLO: all control-plane RPCs must authenticate with mTLS and have audit logs.

Observability and playbooks:
- Telemetry: per-route latency, egress bytes by destination, per-customer routing decisions (for audits), cert issuance events.
- Tracing: propagate trace-id from edge through mesh; ensure sampling of 100% for canaries and 1% normally.
- Runbooks: step-by-step for region failover, including how to drain gateways, update routing weights, and revert.

Rollout checklist (minimum viable):
- [ ] Deploy regional gateway prototype in us-west-2 and eu-west-1 behind Anycast test IP.
- [ ] Implement egress-zone schema and storage (Config DB + API).
- [ ] Wire CA rotation automation for gateway -> mesh re-mTLS.
- [ ] Add telemetry counters for cross-region egress and session-hash collisions.
- [ ] Execute synthetic failover test and record RTO/RPO characteristics.
- [ ] Security review for certificate flows and telemetry PII.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to represent "soft affinity" policies in a user-facing API? (feature request: bind customer to region with fallback cost thresholds)
- Should we allow per-customer Anycast prefixes for enterprise customers who demand dedicated entry points? (bandwidth / IP scarcity tradeoffs)
- Interplay with on-prem Private deployments: what subset of control-plane features must remain local when disconnected?
- eBPF-based fast path for header-based steering vs envoy-level routing: performance testing needed.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally light on implementation details (no concrete BGP / cloud NAT designs) — primary objective is to lock decisions on regional vs central responsibilities, egress zone model, and mTLS termination pattern.
- If we agree on hybrid Anycast + regional control-plane and edge-terminate + re-mTLS to mesh, we can scope an incremental implementation that starts with two regions and expands.

Relevant tickets / refs:
- PLAT-1423: Egress zones schema design
- PLAT-1509: Gateway CA rotation automation
- INFRA-276: Anycast testbed setup

Appendix (short sketches):
- Sketch A: Anycast -> regional gateway -> local mesh -> egress-gateway -> third-party
- Sketch B: Geo-DNS -> regional gateway -> passthrough TLS to sidecar (private deployments)

If you care about perf numbers: initial latency budget at edge termination target: p50 < 8ms, p95 < 30ms (edge processing only), mesh hop adds 5-20ms dependent on region. Cross-region RTTs dominate when cross-region chosen.

Please add comments inline here or link PR to gitlab:infra/edge-config and mention PLAT-1423 when creating follow-ups.

-----
Notes-to-self (quick bullets):
- Keep gateway config immutable where possible; use layer for policy that is easy to roll back.
- Prefer signed, versioned config bundles for gateways (avoid live patching every minute).
- For LLM streaming endpoints, minimize tokenization hops at gateway (avoid re-serialization).

End of doc.
